name: The Gambler's Fallacy
statement: Believing a run of one outcome makes the opposite 'due' in independent trials.
meaning: The mistaken belief that if an independent, equally likely outcome has come up more than expected lately, the other becomes more likely next — that after a run of black, red is 'due'. It is wrong: the wheel has no memory, and each spin keeps its original odds regardless of what came before.
mechanism: It comes from misapplying the law of large numbers to short runs. That law says the proportion of outcomes converges over very many trials; it does not say short sequences must balance out. Believers effectively hold a false 'law of small numbers', expecting a handful of trials to be representative of the long run, when in truth there is no corrective force — early deviations are diluted by volume, not cancelled.

examples.text: At the Monte Carlo Casino on 18 August 1913 the roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row; as the streak grew, gamblers bet ever more heavily on red, wrongly sure the imbalance had to correct, and lost heavily.
Avoiding numbers that just won, or expecting a die face that has been scarce lately — each draw or roll keeps its fixed odds, untouched by the past.
'We've had three girls, so the next must be a boy' misreads roughly independent births as if past children shifted the odds of the next.

variants.name: The hot-hand fallacy
variants.text: The inverse error of expecting a streak to continue rather than reverse — though Miller and Sanjurjo's 2018 work found a selection bias in the classic study, suggesting the hot hand may be partly real.

variants.name: The law of averages
variants.text: The colloquial misconception behind it — the belief in a balancing force that makes outcomes even out in the short run, which is not a real mathematical law.

whyItMatters: It is one of the best-documented reasoning errors about randomness, costly at the roulette table and in every domain where people expect chance to self-correct. Understanding it is understanding that independent events have no memory — the single most common misconception about probability.

working.text: for genuinely independent events, keep the odds fixed regardless of recent runs; nothing is ever 'due'.

working.lead: Check whether events are actually independent
working.text: the fallacy applies only to independent trials; for dependent ones like cards dealt without replacement, adjusting expectations is rational.
resist the sense that a streak must reverse to even things out — that is the false law of averages, not the law of large numbers.

limits: It is a genuine, well-documented cognitive bias, robust in experiments and in real behaviour. Its crucial scope condition is independence: the error is specifically applying 'it's due' reasoning to memoryless independent trials. When events are not independent — sampling without replacement, for instance — adjusting expectations from past outcomes is rational, not fallacious. Its old twin, belief in the hot hand, was itself complicated in 2018 by the discovery of a streak-selection bias, which does not rehabilitate the gambler's fallacy for independent events but unsettles the once-symmetric treatment of the two.
misreadings: It is not a claim that streaks never mean anything — for dependent events, or when a run makes you suspect a biased wheel, updating your expectations can be perfectly rational. The fallacy is strictly the belief that independent, memoryless trials must correct past deviations.
origin: A long-recognised reasoning error, also called the Monte Carlo fallacy after the 1913 roulette run, and studied by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman as a consequence of the representativeness heuristic.

sources.text: Gambler's fallacy, Wikipedia. — the definition, the 1913 Monte Carlo event, the law-of-large-numbers misapplication, and the independence condition.
Miller, J.B. & Sanjurjo, A. (2018). "Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers." Econometrica, 86(6), 2019–2047.
